column4: It names God's single straight path, commands following it, and makes the competing paths disperse walkers from it; this is the section's shared, trodden route versus people going apart.
The Prophet says his Lord guided him to a straight path, an upright dīn; it joins hidaya, sirat, the section's dīn, and q-w-m straightness in one claim.
It assigns the direction of the way to God and says some ways are crooked. Its qasd/direction and crooked branch make the section's line, middle, and deviation concrete.
Moses asks to be guided to sawāʾ al-sabīl, the level or middle of the road, directly realizing the source dictionary sense of the road's middle.
It stages the bewildered person in the earth, with companions calling him back to guidance; this is the section's dalle fi al-ard scene and its communal answer.
God calls to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, making hidaya show both the route and the destination or home.
Mountains, rivers, and roads are placed in the earth so people may find their way; the route is read through the terrain the section calls its signs.
Its signs and star-guidance give the Quranic scene for the section's source dictionary sense of alama/alamin as a landmark used to find a road.
The stars are made so people can be guided through the darknesses of land and sea, extending the section's landmark-and-navigation scene beyond 16:16.
For every qawm there is a hadi. It gives the source image of a guide who goes before a people and the qawm that follows a concrete Quranic form.
Abraham tells his father, Follow me, and promises to guide him to a sound path. The speaker literally takes the prior position of the hadi in the section.
Jesus joins worship of the one Lord to the declaration that this is a straight path, making na'budu's worship the way itself.
Jesus again commands worship of God and calls it the straight path, preserving the section's worship-path equation in its own speech.
Jesus' command to worship God is again completed by this is a straight path; its repeated formulation makes worship the route rather than merely a doctrine.
The divine address says Worship Me; this is a straight path. It directly links the fifth-ayah worship to the sixth-ayah road.
The bee is told to follow its Lord's paths made dhululan, made easy or subdued. That concrete traversable path meets the source's secondary image of a softened, tamed walking surface.
The Prophet calls this my way, and includes those who follow him. It supplies both the leading caller and the people walking a shared route behind him.
God makes Abraham's household leaders who guide by His command; their leadership gives a Quranic form to the section's front-going hadi.
Patient and certain Israelites are made leaders guiding by God's command. The verse binds ongoing steadfastness to a community's guiding leaders.
The believing man tells his qawm, Follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct. This is the section's guide-ahead-of-a-community scene in direct speech.
God guides whom He wills to a straight path; its exact path-and-guidance formulation carries the Fatiha petition into the change of qibla.
After human beings become divided, God guides believers to the truth they dispute by His permission, to a straight path. It places a single guided route after communal division.
Holding fast to God is followed by being guided to a straight path, joining a sustaining grip to the continued route requested in the section.
Obedience to God and the Messenger would bring the promise of guidance to a straight path; the verse makes following the leader a route to that path.
It identifies the obedient as being with those upon whom God bestowed favor, including prophets and the righteous. It concretely identifies the favored company in Fatiha 1:7, after 4:68's path.
Those who hold fast to God receive mercy and are guided to Him on a straight path; the endpoint and route remain together.
God guides those seeking His pleasure along paths of peace and out of darkness, then to a straight path; it makes guidance an actual passage with a destination.
God may leave someone in darkness or set that person on a straight path. The paired placement makes the path a condition one is put upon, not merely knows about.
After naming a gathered line of prophets and their fathers and descendants, the verse says God chose and guided them to a straight path: a predecessor community already walking it.
The Prophet is commanded to follow the guidance of the preceding prophets. It is an explicit Quranic version of walking a route already made by those before.
God calls this the straight path of your Lord and says the signs have been detailed for a people who remember, linking a road with the signs that make it legible.

Moses and Aaron are told to remain upright and not follow the way of those who do not know. Its command to persist realizes the source dictionary sense of staying in one's course without turning aside.
After saying every creature is held by its forelock, Hud says his Lord is upon a straight path. The straightness is the dependable line of divine rule over those moving within it.
The Prophet and those who repent with him are ordered to remain upright as commanded and not overstep. It gives the section's continuing, communal walking its imperative form.
Joseph calls exclusive worship the upright dīn. The explicit pairing of dīn with q-w-m straightness develops the section's secondary sense of dīn as a sustained way or practice.
The Book brings people from darkness into light by their Lord's permission, to the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy. Guidance here crosses a real before-and-after passage.
The messengers say God has guided us to our paths. Their plural paths are the routes on which they then endure harm, combining guidance and continued travel.
God calls this a straight path to Me. It gives the section's hidaya image of a road whose destination is known, rather than direction without arrival.
In its contrast between two men, the one who commands justice is upon a straight path. The path marks a public, active line of conduct rather than a private claim.
Abraham is chosen and guided to a straight path. His exemplary, grateful course becomes a named antecedent for the community-and-favor strand of the section.
When God's guidance comes, whoever follows it will neither go astray nor suffer. It states the direct opposite of the section's dal-lost traveler as sustained following.
The closing question distinguishes the companions of the even path and the guided. It makes straightness and being guided a matter revealed at the route's outcome.
They are guided to good speech and to the path of the Praiseworthy. The verse preserves the twofold hidaya of right utterance and a route to its Lord.
God is the guide of believers to a straight path. In context, recognizing the revealed truth is what lets them take that route.
The Messenger is said to call people to a straight path. The verse supplies the calling, forward-facing guide which the section's hadi image requires.
After clear signs are sent down, God guides whom He wills to a straight path. The signs are the disclosed markers through which that path is known.
God guides travelers through the darknesses of land and sea. This is a second navigation scene for the landmarks and signs of the section, now with the guide named explicitly.
Those who strive for God are promised guidance to His ways. The plural ways are reached through persevering movement, rather than by a detached assertion of belief.
Those given knowledge see the revelation as truth that guides to the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy. It pairs a readable sign with the road it discloses.
Its declaration that Muhammad is a messenger supplies the guide-speaker; the immediately following 36:4 gives that messenger's own standing on the straight path.
It says the messenger is upon a straight path. Its own contribution is to locate the leader announced in 36:3 on the route he communicates.
Moses and Aaron are guided to a straight path after receiving the clear Book, linking a named pair of leaders, scripture, and a traveled line.
The Messenger declares the one God and commands people to be upright toward Him. The imperative gives the section's straight continuation a direct address.
Those who say our Lord is God and then remain upright receive the angels' reassurance. Straightness is presented as a course sustained after the first confession.
The Prophet is commanded to call and remain upright as commanded. It makes his own firmness part of his leading call to the route.
The Prophet is said to guide to a straight path, directly joining prophetic speech and the section's front-going hadi.
The Prophet is told to hold fast to revelation because he is upon a straight path. Holding and remaining on it make the route continuous rather than momentary.
The Prophet is placed on a sharia, a way of command, and told to follow it rather than desires. Its way becomes the daily dīn-like practice that resists departure.
Those who say our Lord is God and remain upright need not fear or grieve. The verse repeats the enduring straight stance as a lived course.
The jinn describe the revealed Book as guiding to truth and a straight path. It gives the Book the road-disclosing function of the section's signs.
Along with forgiveness and completing favor, God guides the Prophet to a straight path. Favor and the route meet here as they do in Fatiha 1:7.
Had people remained steadfast upon the way, they would have received abundant water. Its conditional uses a path as something one can stay on and receive provision along.
God says He showed the human being the way, whether grateful or ungrateful. The shown route has the same active disclosure requested by ihdina.
It says the person who exchanges faith for disbelief has gone astray from sawāʾ al-sabīl. The exact middle-of-the-road expression reverses Moses' request in 28:22.
One who follows a course other than the believers' way is turned toward what he chose. It gives a boundary for the section's shared community path.
Those who lead others astray are said to have strayed from sawāʾ al-sabīl. It is the same road-middle vocabulary as 28:22, now as a missed line.
Iblis vows to sit upon God's straight path for people. The road is not empty: the lost-way danger takes the form of an ambush on the very route requested in Fatiha.
It specifies the attack as from before, behind, right, and left. As the continuation of 7:16, its four directions surround the section's straight traveler without replacing the road itself.
The people are forbidden to sit on every road threatening travelers, blocking God's way, and seeking it crooked. It reverses the guide and landmark scene into obstruction and distortion.
Those who reject God's signs do not take the way of right conduct when they see it, but take the way of error. The verse makes the divergent choice between visible routes explicit.
Pharaoh leads his people astray and does not guide them. This is the counter-image to the hadi who goes ahead of a qawm.
Those who do not believe in the Hereafter deviate from the straight path. It gives the opposing route of the people to whom 23:73 is calling.
At judgment people say their chiefs and great ones made them lose the way. The community's leaders here do the opposite of the preceding guide.
The criminals are told to separate today. Its own judgment-day partition completes the route boundary stated in 36:61, rather than merely repeating its worship command.
The devil has led a great multitude astray. It names the destructive guide and scattered human mass that follow the worship-path warning of 36:61.
The command to guide them to the path of Hell reverses both hidaya and the destination of the straight path: the same road-language reaches the contrary home.
David is warned not to follow desire, lest it lead him away from God's way. Desire is the force that bends a ruler off the line he must keep straight.
Pharaoh claims that he guides his people only to the way of right conduct. Its false guide-speech is answered by the believer's genuine Follow me in 40:38.
Thamud are shown guidance but prefer blindness to it. The refusal turns the section's readable signs into a chosen failure of orientation.
The speakers claim that they found their fathers on a community and are guided by their traces. Their inherited footprints form a contrary test for the section's already-walked path.
The same claim is repeated of later affluent communities: they follow the traces of their fathers. It makes custom's repeated track a possible substitute for actual guidance.
After guidance has become clear, some turn back on their heels. The bodily reversal gives a concrete opposite to staying in the course one has taken.
It compares one walking face-down, stumbling, with one walking upright upon a straight path. The physical traveler makes the section's path image visible in reverse and fulfillment.
God says He showed the two high roads. The disclosed alternatives give the request for a guided way its moral fork.
God finds the Prophet dāll and guides him. The compact reversal is the source's hidaya-versus-dalal pair, with the latter overcome rather than inhabited.
After the descent, whoever follows God's guidance need not fear or grieve. It adds the ongoing act of following to the section's request to be led.
The community is told to hold God's rope all together and not become divided. Its shared holding gives a communal counterpoint to the section's people scattering in every direction.
God promises to make clear and guide believers in the sunan of those before them. These prior courses specify the idea of a route already trodden by earlier people.
Among Moses' people is a community that guides by the truth and judges with it. It supplies a qawm whose collective activity is guidance, rather than merely being guided.
A community created by God guides by truth and acts justly with it. Its corporate guidance extends the section's association of a road with a people.
The question contrasts one who guides to truth with one unable to guide unless guided. It tests who may genuinely occupy the section's role of hadi.
The ruined settlement remains on an established road. A continuing public route carries a visible sign for those who pass it, connecting road and readable trace.
The two punished peoples are said to lie by a clear imam, an open route. With 15:76 it keeps the road as the place where past signs remain available to travelers.
The Quran guides to what is aqwam, more upright. Its q-w-m form gives the section's straightness a superlative moral direction.
One blind in this world is blind in the next and farther astray in way. The verse gives a contrary navigation image: inability to see signs becomes loss of route.
It names the prophets and righteous descendants upon whom God bestowed favor. The phrase identifies the favored people of 1:7, before 19:59 shows their successors' break.
Moses and Aaron announce that peace is for whoever follows guidance. Their message makes huda something followed behind a pair of messengers.
Each community has an appointed rite, while the Prophet stands upon straight guidance. The verse ties a practiced communal dīn to a guiding line.
The addressees are told that obedience to the Messenger will bring guidance. It makes following a messenger the concrete response to a guide's call.
The Messenger asks no reward except that whoever wills may take a path to his Lord. It supplies the route-to-the-Lord side of the section's road-and-home sense.
Turn the face toward the upright dīn, the fitra God made. The dīn plus q-w-m pairing develops the section's daily, straightened way of life.
Turn the face toward the upright dīn before the irreversible day arrives. It makes keeping one's orientation a sustained preparation, not a bare label.
After refusing parents' call to shirk, one is told to follow the way of one who turns to God. It specifies a human route to follow while setting a boundary for inherited obedience.
Luqman tells his son to be moderate in his walking. The concrete gait gives a small bodily analogue to the section's middle and un-deviating route.
Abraham says he is going to his Lord and that He will guide him. The journey makes guidance point toward the Lord as a known destination.
The commanded dīn is to be established and not divided within. Its continuity and refusal of fragmentation parallel the section's single shared way against scattered groups.
The command to worship sincerely is called the dīn al-qayyima. The source's dīn and q-w-m senses meet here in an enacted, upright practice.
